strengths: Introduces a well-motivated Bayesian Beta-Binomial framework for modeling expert behavior in L2D that naturally supports prior incorporation, uncertainty quantification, and adaptation to unseen experts without meta-learning machinery, addressing clear limitations of the L2D-Pop baseline.

Provides theoretical backing (Propositions 1-3) with convergence guarantees and sample complexity bounds for correctly identifying expert competence classes, which is a valuable and relatively rare addition to the L2D literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six diverse datasets (including several realistic medical imaging benchmarks) and multiple expert-diversity regimes (overlap probability p = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8), with both ID and OOD expert settings.

Proposes new evaluation metrics (AURSAC, AURDAC) that generalize accuracy-rejection curves to account for variable deferral budgets, addressing a genuine gap in how L2D systems are typically evaluated with a single system-accuracy number.

Demonstrates a practically useful capability -- incorporating self-assessed expert priors -- that, to the authors' knowledge, is novel in the L2D literature, and shows both benefits (accurate priors) and risks (inaccurate priors) empirically.
Reduces reliance on dense expert annotation of the full training/query set, a practical improvement over prior L2D approaches requiring complete expert-label pairs.

Reports consistent and often substantial performance gains over L2D-Pop, Pop-Avg, and Multi-Expert L2D baselines, particularly in OOD expert and high-diversity settings, with results averaged over multiple seeds.
weaknesses: The synthetic expert simulation protocol (oracle for expertise class plus uniform overlap probability p for other classes) produces experts whose behavior is, by construction, fully captured by class-conditional accuracy -- exactly the sufficient statistic the Beta-Binomial model estimates. This creates a strong alignment (arguably circularity) between the expert generative process and the model's inductive bias, which may inflate the apparent advantage of EA-L2D over baselines that do not make this same assumption.

The core modeling assumption that expert competence can be reduced to a single per-class accuracy value (ignoring instance-level or feature-dependent variation in expert accuracy) is restrictive and likely unrealistic for real clinical experts, where accuracy depends heavily on case difficulty within a class, not just the class label itself.

Despite strong motivation around healthcare and patient safety, no experiments use real human expert annotations; all reported results rely on simulated experts, which limits the strength of claims about real-world applicability and clinical relevance.

The related work section extensively discusses limited-annotation L2D methods (Hemmer et al. 2023, Anonymous 2024, Alves et al. 2024) but none of these are included as empirical baselines, leaving open whether EA-L2D's annotation efficiency actually outperforms these more directly comparable methods.

The prior-incorporation experiment (Section 5.3) is limited to a single dataset and a single class scenario, offering only a narrow demonstration of a claimed key contribution; broader ablations (e.g., varying prior strength s, multiple classes/datasets, sensitivity analysis) are missing.

No analysis of computational cost, model complexity, or training/inference time comparisons against baselines, despite claims of the method being simpler/less cumbersome than the meta-learning-based L2D-Pop.
Details on how statistical significance (bolded results) was determined are not provided in the main text, reducing the interpretability/reproducibility of the comparative claims.

The multi-expertise experiment (Section 5.2) is limited to two datasets and a small set of synthetic multi-class experts, providing only modest evidence for robustness to more complex, realistic expert profiles.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in L2D literature: handling experts with unseen expertise at test time without expensive meta-learning or retraining, motivated clearly against L2D-Pop.

The Bayesian Beta-Binomial formulation is a reasonably principled way to summarize per-class expert accuracy and naturally supports incorporating informative priors, which is a novel capability relative to prior L2D work.
Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning six datasets, including several medical imaging modalities with class imbalance, plus ID/OOD expert splits and varying expert overlap probabilities.
Proposes new AURSAC/AURDAC metrics that generalize accuracy-rejection curves to variable deferral budgets, which could be a useful evaluation tool for the community.
Reports consistent empirical gains over L2D-Pop, Pop-Avg and Multi-Expert L2D baselines across most settings, particularly for OOD/specialized experts.
weaknesses: The experimental setup relies entirely on synthetic experts that are, by construction, oracles for a single 'expertise class' and near-random/uniformly accurate otherwise. This generative process is essentially identical to the inductive bias baked into the proposed Beta-Binomial per-class accuracy model, creating a strong risk of circularity: the method is evaluated almost exclusively on data that matches its own modeling assumptions, inflating apparent gains over baselines that do not share this assumption as explicitly.

Despite the paper's strong emphasis on healthcare and high-stakes applications, no real human expert annotations are used for any dataset (including the medical ones) — all expert behavior is simulated. This substantially weakens claims about practical applicability and robustness to real expert behavior, which is typically far noisier and context/instance-dependent rather than cleanly separable by class.

The core assumption that expert accuracy is well summarized by a single per-class scalar (ignoring instance-level difficulty or feature-dependent competence) is a significant simplification that is not tested against more realistic, instance-dependent expert noise models or real-world expert datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10H, NIH ChestXray with radiologist labels) that are available in the L2D literature.

The theoretical contributions (Propositions 1–3) are direct, fairly standard applications of the Law of Large Numbers and Hoeffding's inequality to a Beta-Binomial posterior; they provide limited additional insight beyond confirming basic consistency of empirical/posterior mean estimation, and do not meaningfully strengthen the paper's central claims about deferral quality.

The empirical comparison omits several more recent and directly relevant baselines explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., Mao et al. 2023/2024, Hemmer et al. 2023, Alves et al. 2024, the EM-based missing-annotation method), leaving only three comparators, one of which (Pop-Avg) is a simple baseline introduced by the authors themselves, which weakens the strength of the state-of-the-art comparison.

Statistical significance is claimed in table captions ('bold indicates statistically significant best result') but no test, significance level, or methodology for this determination is described anywhere in the main text or appendix.

The 'expert-agnostic' terminology is somewhat misleading: the system still constructs an explicit per-expert behavioral representation R_E; the actual novelty is a lightweight, non-parametric/Bayesian representation versus a meta-learned one, which is a narrower and less striking contribution than the framing suggests.

The reduced-annotation mechanism (Section 4.3), which approximates expert predictions via the estimated expertise class E*, is only lightly validated — there is no ablation isolating how much of the performance gain stems from this approximation versus the Bayesian representation itself, nor a quantification of how annotation savings trade off against deferral accuracy as context data shrinks further.

The multi-expertise experiment (Section 5.2) is limited to only two datasets and a toy two-expert setup, which is too narrow to convincingly demonstrate robustness to experts with multiple genuine areas of competence—an important real-world scenario the paper claims to address.

Given the heavy reliance on synthetic, class-oracle experts and the lack of any real-world expert-annotated evaluation, the reported 1-16% / 4-28% performance gains may not generalize to realistic deployment settings, undermining the practical significance of the claimed contributions.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated Bayesian Beta-Binomial approach to model expert behaviour that naturally supports incorporating prior knowledge, an underexplored capability in prior L2D literature.
Provides theoretical grounding (Propositions 1-3 with proofs) establishing convergence guarantees and sample complexity bounds for correctly identifying expert accuracy/expertise.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six diverse datasets (CIFAR-10, HAM10000, GTSRB, Breast Ultrasound, Axial Organ Slices, Blood Cell MNIST) spanning general vision, medical imaging, and high-class-count settings.
Proposes new evaluation metrics (AURSAC, AURDAC) that address a real limitation of standard system accuracy for comparing deferral systems across variable deferral budgets.
Demonstrates substantial and consistent gains for out-of-distribution (unseen) experts over the main comparator L2D-Pop, directly addressing the stated motivation of the paper.
Reduces reliance on expert annotations across the full training query set, which is a practically meaningful contribution given the cost of expert labels.

Additional ablations (varying expert population diversity, multi-expertise experts, and prior informativeness) strengthen the empirical narrative and probe the method's behaviour under different regimes.
weaknesses: All experiments use synthetic/simulated 'oracle-style' experts (perfect on expertise class, uniform-random or fixed overlap probability elsewhere); this is a strong and somewhat unrealistic simplification of real human expert behaviour (e.g., correlated errors, non-uniform confusion patterns), and no real human-annotated expert data is used to validate the approach.

The core modelling assumption that each expert has crisp, single/multi-class 'expertise' with per-class independent Beta-distributed accuracy may not capture more nuanced or correlated real-world expertise patterns, limiting external validity.

At low expert diversity (p=0.8), gains over L2D-Pop and even Pop-Avg largely vanish or reverse (L2D-Pop is bolded as best in several p=0.8 rows), suggesting the reported 1-16%/4-28% gains in the abstract are concentrated in specific (high-diversity) regimes and may overstate general applicability.

Baselines are limited to L2D-Pop, a self-constructed 'Pop-Avg' baseline, and Multi-Expert L2D (inapplicable to OOD); no empirical comparison to other cited limited-annotation methods (Hemmer et al. 2023, Alves et al. 2024, Anonymous 2024) that are directly relevant to the paper's claimed contribution of reduced annotation reliance.

The prior-incorporation experiment (Section 5.3) is a single simple simulated scenario on one dataset/class, offering limited evidence for how well the approach would perform with realistic, imperfectly calibrated human self-assessments, despite this being framed as a key contribution.
No analysis of computational/training efficiency compared to the meta-learning-based L2D-Pop, despite claiming to 'bypass the cumbersome meta-learning process' as an advantage.

Sensitivity to context set size (which varies per dataset somewhat arbitrarily) is not systematically studied, leaving open how robust the Bayesian estimates are under very small or unbalanced per-class context samples in practice.
It is unclear how statistical significance of bolded 'best' results is computed, which affects confidence in the comparative claims across many tables.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: identifies concrete limitations of the SOTA L2D-Pop method (OOD generalization, heavy annotation requirements, no mechanism for prior expert knowledge) and proposes a principled alternative.

Strong theoretical grounding: the Beta-Binomial Bayesian representation comes with convergence guarantees (Prop. 1), sample-complexity bounds for overcoming prior misspecification (Prop. 2), a formal expert-agnosticism invariance proof (Prop. 3), and an asymptotic characterization of the induced Bayes-optimal decision rule (Thm C.3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four diverse medical imaging datasets and multiple expert-diversity settings (p=0.2/0.5/0.8), with both ID and OOD expert evaluation and appropriate statistical significance testing.

Good set of baselines (L2D-Pop, Pop-Avg, Multi-Expert L2D) and multiple research questions addressing robustness, multi-expertise scaling, prior knowledge utility, context-data scaling, and input distribution shift (BCN20000).

Practical advantages clearly demonstrated: substantially reduced expert annotation requirements (context-only vs. context+query), and qualitative/computational efficiency arguments supported by a t-SNE analysis showing L2D-Pop's latent embeddings entangle and overfit to ID experts.

Thorough ablation study (LCB weighting) with carefully designed synthetic expert types (high/low-skill, high/low-uncertainty) that supports the specific design choice of uncertainty-aware weighting in the loss.
Clear method exposition with an intuitive figure-based walkthrough (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) of how the expert representation and rejector interact.
weaknesses: All experiments rely entirely on simulated experts with synthetic accuracy/overlap noise models; no real human-expert data is used to validate the central claims about generalization to genuinely unseen expert behavior, which is a significant limitation for a paper motivated by human-AI collaboration in high-stakes domains.

The per-class Beta-Binomial representation is coarse: it assumes expert accuracy is uniform within a class and ignores instance-level or feature-dependent variation in expert competence, correlations between classes, and complex error patterns (acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically probed against more nuanced synthetic expert behaviors).

Reported gains in Table 1 are often small and non-significant in several ID and higher-overlap (p=0.8) settings; the headline '28% relative improvement' appears to reflect a few favorable low-p/OOD cases rather than a consistent effect across the full experimental grid, which could be presented more conservatively.

The claimed computational efficiency advantage over L2D-Pop (Appendix A.3) is argued analytically via asymptotic complexity but not empirically validated with actual wall-clock training/inference time comparisons.

The method still requires a non-trivial number of training experts (J) to learn a generalizable rejector rϕ; the paper does not clearly analyze how performance depends on the diversity/number of training experts, which is important given the meta-learning-like nature of the training procedure despite the 'expert-agnostic' framing.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to L2D-Pop: the core idea (replace learned latent expert embeddings with explicit Bayesian per-class statistics) is a reasonable but conceptually straightforward substitution, and much of the paper's bulk is devoted to supporting theory/appendices rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas.

The rejector's expert-agnostic invariance proof (Prop. 3) is somewhat definitional (identical inputs yield identical outputs for any function), and the practical significance beyond Remark A.1's informal argument about continuity is not rigorously quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem in L2D: robustness to out-of-distribution experts at test time, which has clear practical relevance for high-stakes domains like healthcare.

The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough: four datasets, multiple overlap probabilities (expert diversity), ID/OOD splits, several research questions (RQ1-RQ5), and an ablation on the LCB weighting term.

The paper provides theoretical analysis (convergence of posterior means, sample-complexity bounds for overcoming prior misspecification, and an asymptotic characterisation of the induced deferral rule), which is a nice complement to the empirical results.
The qualitative t-SNE analysis of L2D-Pop's latent space (Section 5.4) offers an intuitive, plausible explanation for why latent-embedding approaches may overfit to ID experts.

Practical advantages such as reduced annotation requirements (context-only vs. context+query) and lower computational cost relative to meta-learning-based L2D-Pop are reasonable and partially substantiated (Appendix A.3).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is fairly thin: the method essentially computes per-class Beta-Binomial posterior accuracy estimates and feeds a handful of scalar statistics (at the predicted class and the expert's best class) into a small MLP rejector. This is a relatively simple statistical technique, and the extensive theoretical machinery (three propositions, multiple appendix proofs) mostly formalises fairly standard results (law of large numbers, Hoeffding bounds, convex combination of prior/posterior means) rather than providing deep new insight.

Proposition 3 ("expert-agnosticism") is close to a tautology: it shows that if the same six numerical inputs are fed into the same function rϕ, the output is identical. This is true by construction of the input design and does not constitute a substantive theoretical guarantee about generalisation; it does not establish that the learned rϕ will actually behave sensibly on truly novel statistical profiles, only that symbolically identical inputs yield identical outputs.

All experiments use fully synthetic/simulated experts, generated by a single primary expertise class with a fixed overlap probability p. This generative process maps almost exactly onto the representational assumptions of EA-L2D (independent per-class Beta accuracy), which plausibly biases the comparison in the proposed method's favour relative to L2D-Pop, which must learn this structure implicitly via meta-learning from predictions rather than having it baked into its representation. The paper does not include any real multi-expert dataset, which is a significant limitation for a method motivated by high-stakes medical deployment.

The deferral mechanism only ever looks at statistics for two classes (the classifier's top prediction k* and the expert's single "best" class E*), discarding the rest of the K-dimensional representation R^E. This seems like a significant architectural bottleneck when expert competence is not well summarised by a single peak class, and the multi-expertise experiment (RQ2) does not clearly address whether this bottleneck limits performance in more complex, realistic expertise patterns.

The core approximation in the loss (replacing the true deferral condition m=y with the coarse proxy E*=y, i.e., whether the query's class matches the expert's historically best class) discards per-instance information about whether the expert would actually get this specific case right, which could be a poor proxy for experts whose correctness varies with instance difficulty even within their area of expertise.

Statistical testing is done pairwise across many conditions (datasets × overlap levels × ID/OOD) without clear correction for multiple comparisons, and sample sizes (10 expert cohorts) are modest, raising some concern about the robustness of the significance claims in Table 1 and Figures 3/8.

The “expert-agnostic” framing is somewhat oversold rhetorically (e.g., parallels drawn to MAML, TAML, Agnostic Federated Learning in §2 and Appendix A.2.1) relative to what is actually demonstrated, which amounts to the rejector not seeing raw class labels as input features — a fairly modest architectural choice rather than a deep methodological innovation comparable to the cited meta-learning/fairness literature.

Considerable redundancy exists between the main text and the appendix (e.g., Appendix A.1/A.2 largely restate §4's motivations in more verbose form), suggesting the paper may be padded to meet length/complexity expectations rather than containing proportionate novel content.

strengths: The paper addresses well-motivated and practically important limitations of prior L2D-to-population work (L2D-Pop): OOD generalisation failure, heavy annotation requirements, and lack of a mechanism to inject prior expert knowledge.

The proposed Bayesian (Beta-Binomial) representation of expert competence is simple, interpretable, and efficient, and the paper provides solid theoretical backing (Propositions 1-3, Theorem C.3) with rigorous proofs in the appendix that connect the design choices to concrete guarantees (consistency of expertise-class identification, sample complexity for overcoming prior misspecification, and Bayes-consistency/expert-agnosticism of the resulting decision rule).

Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse medical imaging datasets and multiple expert diversity settings (p=0.2/0.5/0.8), with appropriate baselines (L2D-Pop, Pop-Avg, Multi-Expert L2D) and statistically tested results (paired t-tests), consistently shows EA-L2D matching or exceeding SOTA on ID experts and substantially outperforming on OOD experts.

Good range of supporting analyses beyond the main comparison: multi-expertise scaling (RQ2), prior-knowledge/context interaction (RQ3), context-pool scaling (RQ4, appendix), input-distribution shift robustness using an independent dataset (RQ5/BCN20000), and a targeted LCB-weighting ablation isolating the uncertainty-awareness contribution.

The qualitative t-SNE analysis of L2D-Pop's latent space (Fig. 5) provides a compelling and interpretable explanation for why the meta-learned latent baseline overfits to ID experts and fails on OOD experts, strengthening the causal narrative behind the empirical gains.

Practical advantages are clearly and honestly quantified: substantially reduced annotation burden (context-only vs. context+query) and lower computational cost (avoiding per-query attention over context sets), both argued analytically in the appendix.

The paper is transparent about limitations (sensitivity to badly misspecified priors under sparse data, potentially coarser representation than fine-grained latent embeddings) rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on simulated experts (synthetic overlap-probability behaviour) rather than real human expert predictions; while this follows prior work's protocol and is justified by data availability, it somewhat limits external validity and the practical claims about real-world deployment.

The core theoretical guarantees (Propositions 1-3, Theorem C.3) rely on asymptotic/idealized conditions (e.g., context samples nk to infinity, i.i.d. class-wise accuracy assumptions treating expert competence as constant per class rather than instance-dependent), and it is not fully clear how tightly these bounds hold or transfer to the practical finite-sample, non-i.i.d. regimes used in experiments.

The Beta-Binomial representation assumes a single scalar accuracy per class, which may be a coarse model of real expert behaviour (e.g., failing to capture input-conditional expert competence or correlations across classes) -- the paper acknowledges this only briefly as a limitation without deeper empirical stress-testing.

The rejector's expert-agnostic input design uses only the classifier's top class and the expert's peak expertise class (plus their paired statistics); it is unclear how this restricted 6-dimensional input scales/generalizes to more complex expert behaviour with several comparably strong specialties or how sensitive results are to this specific choice versus richer inputs.

Some comparisons (e.g., against L2D-Pop) could be more thoroughly tuned/validated -- limited discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity for baselines and whether L2D-Pop was optimally configured for the same context sizes used by EA-L2D.
The writing in places (e.g., abstract/intro) contains minor grammatical roughness that could be polished for a final version, though this does not affect substance.
